Looking at the most recent `ps aux` snapshot I just fetched, the only remaining high‑memory process that isn’t part of the intended “run A” workers (which have PIDs 2547035, 2547033, 2547036) is PID 99826. It’s a Python multiprocessing fork still using ~7 GiB (7.3 % of RAM). This matches the user’s complaint: it’s the “climbing” process that should have been dead.

My goal now is to:

1. Terminate PID 99826 cleanly (SIGTERM) and, if it doesn’t exit promptly, force‑kill it (SIGKILL). A short `sleep 2` gives it a chance to shut down gracefully before the hard kill.
2. Verify that memory usage has dropped after the kill, so I’ll run `free -h | head -2` to show total/used/free again.
3. Provide the user with a small, deterministic piece of output to confirm the command ran (the `grep -c . /dev/null` trick prints “0”, a harmless count).
4. Show that the main “run A” process is still alive and progressing by dumping the tail of its log file (`/tmp/runA_warmup_verify.log`). I’ll limit the output to the last 300 bytes to keep it concise.

All of these steps can be combined into a single Bash command, which the tool interface expects as a JSON object with `command` and `description`. The command will therefore be:

```
kill 99826; sleep 2; kill -9 99826 2>/dev/null; free -h | head -2; grep -c . /dev/null; tail -c 300 /tmp/runA_warmup_verify.log
```

This exactly matches the actions needed and fits the user’s request to eliminate the climbing process while confirming system state afterwards. I’ll now issue this as a Bash tool call.
